title: Prompting as an engineering discipline, not a trick
story:
A prompt is the specification. It is where you state what the system should do, and in most systems it is also the only part that can be changed in under a minute — which is precisely why it gets treated as though it were not really part of the software.

The folklore around it has a specific cause, and naming the cause is more useful than mocking the folklore. Prompt changes are almost always evaluated on one example. You try a phrasing, the answer looks better, you keep it. One example cannot distinguish a real improvement from ordinary variation, so the belief is formed and never tested again. Do that for a few months, with several people, and you have a body of practice nobody can check and nobody can question. That is not a failure of intelligence. It is what happens to any craft that has no measurement, and it would happen to compiler flags or database indexes just as readily.

So the discipline is mostly the ordinary discipline, applied here.

Write the task the way you would write it for a competent stranger who cannot ask you anything. Most disappointing output is a faithful response to an ambiguous instruction, and the ambiguity is invisible to the author because the author knows what they meant. Reading your own prompt as though you did not already know the intention is most of the work, and it is the part that cannot be delegated.

Say what the output must look like, and say what to produce when the task cannot be done. That second clause is the one people leave out, and leaving it out guarantees invention — the pattern of a request followed by a compliant answer is overwhelming, and if no other option is offered the system will produce a compliant answer regardless of whether one exists.

Use examples for what definitions cannot carry, and choose them at the edges rather than the middle. Three comfortable examples teach less than one comfortable example and two awkward ones, because the awkward cases are where behaviour is undetermined and where your real preferences live.

Change one thing at a time, and run the set. Twenty cases with expected properties, runnable in a few minutes, is the entire difference between engineering and taste here. It does not need to be a benchmark, it needs to be repeatable. Before and after, the same twenty, and the question stops being whether it feels better.

Keep it in version control and review it like code, because a prompt change is a behaviour change that ships. The fact that it reads like prose does not make it prose; it is the part of the system that decides what the product does, and the decisions inside it — tone, scope, what to refuse, what to prioritise when two goals conflict — are product decisions that belong somewhere a person can read them. A prompt nobody has read is an undocumented policy.

And treat the model as a dependency with a version, because it is one. A prompt tuned against one version is coupled to that version, and the coupling is invisible until the version changes underneath you. Pin what you can, re-run the set when it moves, and expect some of your phrasing to have been load-bearing for reasons you never knew.

The uncomfortable part of all this is that it is not hard, it is only unglamorous. There is no phrasing that unlocks a better model, and looking for one is how months disappear. What there is: a clear specification, a stated failure output, examples at the edges, a small set of cases, one change at a time, and the same review you would give any other code. Everything in this lesson is available to anyone who decides to stop guessing.

problem.name: Specifying behaviour in natural language
problem.shape: The behaviour of the system is determined by an instruction written in prose, which anyone can edit in a minute.
tell: a phrasing is defended on the strength of one example
nobody can say what the prompt should produce when the task is impossible
the prompt is not in version control, or changes to it are not reviewed
the model version it was tuned against is not recorded anywhere
problem.move: Write the instruction for a competent stranger who cannot ask questions, state the output shape including the failure output, give examples at the edges, then keep twenty cases you re-run before and after every single change.
problem.invariant: A change is only an improvement if the same set of cases is better afterwards — one example cannot separate an improvement from ordinary variation.
problem.breaks: The prompt is coupled to the model version it was tuned against, and that coupling is invisible until the version moves underneath it.

cost.time: a case set has to be built and re-run, which is minutes per change rather than seconds
cost.space: cases and expected properties are a small corpus of their own, to be maintained like any other test data
cost.beats: trying phrasings and keeping what looks better, which accumulates unfalsifiable folklore, and fine-tuning, which is far more expensive and usually unnecessary

worked.problem: Why does prompting collect superstition, and what turns it into engineering?
worked.reasoning:
Because changes get judged on one example, and one example cannot tell an improvement from variation.

The mechanism is worth stating without contempt, since it would happen to any craft in the same position. Someone tries a phrasing, the answer looks better, the belief is formed, and it is never tested again. A few months and a few people later there is a body of practice nobody can check. The problem is the missing measurement, not the people.

What turns it into engineering is ordinary. I write the task as though for a competent stranger who cannot ask me anything, because most bad output is a faithful response to an ambiguous instruction, and the ambiguity is invisible to whoever wrote it. I state the output shape, and specifically what to produce when the task cannot be done — leave that out and invention is guaranteed, because a request followed by a compliant answer is an overwhelming pattern.

Examples carry what definitions cannot, so I choose them at the edges: one comfortable case and two awkward ones teach more than three comfortable ones, because the awkward cases are where behaviour is undetermined.

Then the part that actually does the work. Twenty cases with expected properties, runnable in minutes, re-run before and after every change, with one change at a time. That is the whole difference between engineering and taste here, and it does not need to be a benchmark.

I keep the prompt in version control and review it like code, because it decides what the product does — tone, scope, refusals, which goal wins when two conflict. Those are product decisions and they belong where someone can read them; an unread prompt is an undocumented policy.

And I treat the model as a versioned dependency, because a prompt tuned against one version is coupled to it invisibly. Pin it, re-run the set when it moves, and expect some phrasing to have been load-bearing for reasons nobody knew.

problem.practice: Take your current prompt and twenty real inputs, record what the system produces today, then delete one paragraph of the prompt you assume is essential and run the same twenty again. Either nothing changes, and you have found dead weight, or something breaks, and you have learned what that paragraph was doing. Both outcomes are worth more than another rewrite.

beats.broke: Prompt changes are judged on a single example, which cannot separate an improvement from variation, so unfalsifiable beliefs accumulate into folklore.
beats.fix: Specify the task for a stranger, state the failure output, use edge examples, and keep twenty repeatable cases run before and after every single change.
beats.cost: A case set has to be built and maintained, and the prompt stays coupled to the model version it was tuned against.

interview.q: Why does prompting collect superstition, and what turns it into engineering?
interview.trap: Dismissing it as people being unscientific. The cause is structural — evaluating on one example makes every belief unfalsifiable — and any craft without a measurement develops the same folklore.
interview.answer:
Because a change is judged on one example, and one example cannot separate an improvement from ordinary variation. Someone tries a phrasing, it looks better, the belief forms and is never tested again. A few months of that across a team is a body of practice nobody can check — a missing measurement rather than a failure of intelligence.

What turns it into engineering is unglamorous. Write the task for a competent stranger who cannot ask questions, since most bad output is a faithful response to an ambiguous instruction and the ambiguity is invisible to its author. State the output shape and, specifically, what to produce when the task cannot be done — leave that out and invention is guaranteed, because a request followed by a compliant answer is an overwhelming pattern.

Use examples at the edges rather than the middle, because the awkward cases are where behaviour is undetermined. Then change one thing at a time and re-run twenty cases with expected properties, which takes minutes and is the whole difference between engineering and taste.

I keep it in version control and review it like code, because the decisions inside it — tone, scope, what to refuse, which goal wins in a conflict — are product decisions, and an unread prompt is an undocumented policy. And I treat the model as a versioned dependency, since a prompt tuned against one version is invisibly coupled to it and some phrasing will turn out to have been load-bearing for reasons nobody knew.
